quote: For the 2024 iteration of the program, UCRC officials offered a fixed price per acre-foot that applicants could take or leave — no haggling this time. ... the 2024 program had nearly double the participation, with 109 projects and nearly 64,000 acre-feet of water expected to be conserved.
source_title: Using less of the Colorado River takes a willing farmer and $45 million in federal funds (Aspen Journalism/KUNC, syndicated by KJZZ)

extra_sources.title: Lower Colorado Basin States' Compromise on Water Conservation
extra_sources.quote: To avoid federal government action, California, Arizona, and Nevada created a "Lower Basin Plan," ... agreed to voluntarily conserve three million acre-feet

arithmetic: 2023: 64 projects, ~38,000 AF; 2024: 109 projects, ~64,000 AF. 109/64 = 1.70; 64,000/38,000 = 1.68. Jump minus 1 = 0.70, which equals the model value.
notes: The aspenjournalism.org original is rate-limited (429), so I read the identical syndicated KJZZ copy. The 1.7x jump is confirmed. The article credits it to the fixed take-or-leave price, more lead time and outreach, not to a threat of curtailment, so it is a weak analogue for a mandate. The model's basis says this too. The closest mandate-threat analogue is the 2023 Lower Basin deal: states pledged 3 MAF over 3 years to head off federal cuts proposed in the Draft SEIS. That shows a credible threat moves voluntary volumes, but the source gives no participation multiplier. Nothing published measures this parameter directly. 0.7 borrows the size of a price-design effect.

quote: The program paid about $45 million to participants in 2023 and 2024 combined ... nearly $29 million in payments to water users in 2024 ... about 38,000 acre-feet of water was conserved across the four states, which cost nearly $16 million.
source_title: Using less of the Colorado River takes a willing farmer and $45 million in federal funds
arithmetic: Average price 2023 = $16M/38,000 AF = $421/AF. 2024 = $29M/64,000 AF = $453/AF (ag price posted at ~$500). Quantity ratio 1.68. Implied supply elasticity = ln(1.68)/ln(453/421) = 0.52/0.073 = 7.1, or ln(1.68)/ln(500/421) = 3.0 against the posted price.
notes: The model's scarcity term is (1+held/qRef)^(1/e), so e acts as a supply elasticity. The only observed price-quantity pair (SCPP 2023 to 2024) points to elastic supply (e about 3–7), but program redesign confounds it, so it is not causal. The irrigation-demand meta-analysis (Scheierling et al. 2006, WRR) is still blocked at Wiley and I did not open it, so I quote nothing from it. Suggest raising the high end to about 5. There is no basis to move the central value of 1.

quote: Ceasing alfalfa irrigation early and full-season leasing were the top-performing leasing options, with an average cost of $236 per AF.
locator: Section 5.1 (PDF p.29); Appendix B Table B-8 (PDF p.55): Full Season alfalfa 1.50 AF/acre, $236/AF
source_title: Opportunities and Costs for Agricultural Water Optimization in the Great Salt Lake Basin
publisher: Utah Division of Water Resources (GSL Basin Integrated Plan)

extra_sources.title: Water Banking and Leasing (GSL options brief)
extra_sources.publisher: Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute / GSL Strike Team
extra_sources.quote: Existing water markets suggest the cost per acre-foot may range between $150 and $300.

extra_sources.title: Test program on Price River (Utah SCPP 2023)
extra_sources.quote: Leases conserved an estimated 15,090 acre-feet in 2023 ... Utah farmers received $5.4 million in state and federal funds

extra_sources.title: Using less of the Colorado River takes a willing farmer and $45 million in federal funds
extra_sources.quote: Colorado, Utah and Wyoming paid agricultural water users about $500 an acre-foot

arithmetic: Utah SCPP 2023: $5.4M/15,090 AF = $358/AF. SCPP 2023 all states: $16M/38,000 = $421/AF. Lower Basin 2023: $1.0–1.2B/2.3 MAF = $435–522/AF. GSL-basin figures: $236/AF (state WTA, 2026) and $150–300/AF (Strike Team/Gardner 2023).
notes: $380 matches Colorado River program prices ($358–500/AF). The basis says 'in the basin', and for the GSL basin the 2026 state WTA study and the Strike Team brief both put full-season ag leasing near $236–300/AF of depletion. I suggest $250 (rounded mid of $236 and the $150–300 market range). Keep $380 as a sensitivity case for Colorado-style pricing. HB 410 (2026) sets rates from commodity prices, and the program's first payments come in 2027, so there is no GSL transaction price yet. Sources disagree on units: the DWRe figures are per AF of depletion saved, while SCPP is per AF of conserved consumptive use, so they are broadly comparable.

quote: purchase 942.75 acre-feet of water from LeBaron Ranch Holdings for just over $12,100 per acre-foot, totaling approximately $11,412,997. About 90% of the water purchased from LeBaron Ranch Holdings is dated 1860
source_title: Utah city buys historic water rights for sustainability (Cedar City purchase)

extra_sources.title: Utah wins $30M bid to secure US Magnesium facility, water rights for Great Salt Lake
extra_sources.quote: The winning bid ... would see the Beehive State take ownership of the facility, as well as roughly 144,790 acre-feet of water rights.

extra_sources.title: Utah's effort to save the Great Salt Lake: historic water law, major acquisitions and a federal partnership
extra_sources.quote: purchasing 144,000 acre-feet of water rights annually and other assets for $30 million

extra_sources.title: Water Banking and Leasing
extra_sources.publisher: Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute / GSL Strike Team
extra_sources.quote: Existing water markets suggest the cost per acre-foot may range between $150 and $300.
extra_sources.locator: p.1 (this is an annual LEASE cost, not a purchase price)

arithmetic: US Mag: $30M/144,790 AF = $207/AF (the model's ~$208). Capitalised lease: $250/AF/yr at 3–4% = $6,250–8,300/AF, and $150/yr at 5% = $3,000/AF. Cedar City: $12,100/AF (southern Utah, municipal buyer, 1860 priority).
notes: The 'Utah figures an order of magnitude lower' are not comparable sale prices. The ~$208/AF is a bankruptcy-auction price for brine-extraction rights, bundled with a defunct Superfund-site plant, and it did not buy consumptive ag water. The ~$250 figure is the Strike Team's annual lease cost ($150–300/AF/yr), not a capital price. Capitalising Utah lease rates gives about $3,000–8,300/AF, and the one documented arm's-length Utah purchase of senior ag rights is $12,100/AF (municipal buyer, so an upper bound). $6,000 is consistent with the Utah evidence. The low of $250 is implausible for consumptive ag rights, so I suggest low about $3,000 and high about $12,000. A Wasatch Front or Bear River ag-right transaction series (WestWater) was not found publicly.

quote: the Bureau of Reclamation initially said it would cap payments at $650 per acre-foot, then later revised it down to $595 for farmers like Cotner who raise alfalfa to sell, and $621 for those who grow alfalfa to feed their own cattle herds.
source_title: Test program on Utah's Price River (SCPP)

extra_sources.title: Opportunities and Costs for Agricultural Water Optimization in the GSL Basin
extra_sources.quote: Delaying the start of irrigation (split-season leasing scenarios 3-6) had moderate cost-effectiveness, with costs ranging from $340 to $371 per AF.

arithmetic: Highest observed ag lease payment $650/AF = 1.7x of $380, or 2.6x of a $250 base. The model ceiling is 6 x $380 = $2,280/AF, about 3.5x the highest observed lease payment.
notes: This is a policy cap, so evidence only bounds it. Observed lease prices top out at roughly 1.5–2.6x the base. Capitalised M&I purchase prices ($12,100/AF at 4%, about $480/yr) also sit under 2x. A ceiling of 6 is permissive and is rarely binding against observed data. A central value of about 2–3 would match observed scarcity premia. The irrigation_elasticity_meta source is still blocked and was not opened.

quote: The State pays an average rate of 1.82% on outstanding GO debt. ... several factors make additional debt less attractive at present, including higher long-term interest rates

extra_sources.title: PTIF Portfolio Statistics as of December 31, 2025
PTIF Portfolio Statistics as of June 30, 2025

arithmetic: Range runs from the legacy average GO coupon (1.82%) to the state's cash opportunity cost (PTIF 4.0–4.5%). The midpoint is about 3%.
notes: The cited gsl_commissioner page has no interest rate (I checked the text). The 1.82% is the weighted rate on old GO debt, mostly issued in 2010–2020 at low rates (the 2020 issue had a 1.595% TIC). The Treasurer notes higher long-term rates now, and the state earns about 4% on idle cash in the PTIF, which is the true opportunity cost of instalment payments. New 15–20-yr AAA GO debt in 2025–26 would price well above 1.5%, but I found no recent Utah GO TIC to quote. I suggest 3%, range 1.8–4.5%.

quote: A special tabulation of 2012 Census of Agriculture data for more than two thousand Utah farms revealed yields ranging from under 1 ton to more than 12 tons per acre. The median yield was 3.4 tons, and the average was 4 tons per acre.
locator: Appendix B.1.1.5, PDF p.50–51; Tables B-2 and B-3
source_title: Opportunities and Costs for Agricultural Water Optimization in the Great Salt Lake Basin
arithmetic: Acreage-weighted yield classes (Table B-2 acres x Table B-3 yields): mean 4.02 t/ac. Lowest third of acres (all 2-cut ground plus part of 4-cut flood) averages 3.10 t/ac, so 1 - 3.10/4.02 = 0.23 below the mean. This ignores within-class spread, so the true figure is larger. For a normal distribution the bottom-third mean is mu - 1.09 sigma, so 0.26 implies a yield CV of 0.24. Median/mean = 3.4/4.0 shows right skew.
notes: The 2026 state yield classes support a bottom-third discount of about 0.23 or more, so 0.26 is reasonable. Caveat: repossession through eminent domain requires just compensation at fair market value, so the discount must come from selecting low-value ground, not from paying under market. I did not open the Utah condemnation statutes. Neither cited NASS source page gives a yield distribution.

quote: To reach the minimum healthy lake elevation (4,198 feet) by 2055, mean annual inflows would likely need to be ~2,465 KAF. Between 2000 and 2025, inflows averaged 1,665 KAF per year.
locator: Figure 11 sidebar 'Inflows needed to reach healthy lake elevations', PDF p.24 (report p.4 of section)
source_title: Great Salt Lake Data and Insights Summary
arithmetic: Required added mean inflow = 2,465 - 1,665 = 800 KAF/yr at the lake. A 1,100 KAF/yr mandated cut delivers 800 KAF only if about 73% of it reaches the lake (800/1,100).
notes: This is a policy choice. The state's updated water budget puts the whole recovery gap at about 800 KAF/yr of added inflow, so a 1,100 KAF/yr mandate floor is roughly the full gap grossed up for delivery losses. It is an upper-end sizing, because the model's mandate only covers what voluntary levers miss. The Strike Team calls the scenarios 'not prescriptive'.

quote: Last year Utah's governor, Spencer Cox, pledged to refill the Great Salt Lake by 2034, when the city is slated to host the winter Olympic games.

extra_sources.title: Great Salt Lake Data and Insights Summary
extra_sources.quote: To reach the minimum healthy lake elevation (4,198 feet) by 2055

extra_sources.title: Lower Colorado Basin States' Compromise on Water Conservation
extra_sources.quote: agreed to voluntarily conserve three million acre-feet of water over the next three years

arithmetic: From 2026: the 2034 pledge is about 8 years and the 2055 planning horizon is about 29 years. The Lower Basin cut was phased over 3 years.
notes: This is a policy choice. Published targets bound it between about 8 years (political pledge) and 29 years (Strike Team horizon), so 10 years sits near the aggressive end. The cited Distribution Management Plan page (waterrights.utah.gov homepage text) has no phase-in figure. I tried California SGMA's 20-year statutory phase-in as an analogue, but its pages were blocked or empty, so it is not used.

quote: HAY, ALFALFA 480,000 [acres harvested] 4.3 TONS / ACRE 2,064,000 TONS 176 $ / TON 359,136,000
locator: 2025 State Agriculture Overview, Utah, Crops table

extra_sources.title: Opportunities and Costs for Agricultural Water Optimization in the GSL Basin
extra_sources.quote: Full season leasing yields the largest reduction in depletion per acre—1.5 AF/acre
extra_sources.locator: App. B.1.1.10, PDF p.55; benchmark price '$212 per ton' 25-yr avg, PDF p.50

arithmetic: Revenue per acre (2025) = $359.136M / 480,000 ac = $748/ac (4.3 t x $174 effective). Divided by alfalfa ET of about 3.05 ft gives $245/AF (the model value). Divided by 2.64 AF/ac application gives $283. Divided by the 1.5 AF/ac depletion actually saved by fallowing (DWRe 2026) gives $499/AF. With the 25-yr average price ($212 x 4.0 t = $848/ac): $278/AF at 3.05 ft, $565/AF at 1.5 AF/ac.
notes: The cited NASS Utah landing page has no figures, so I used the NASS 2025 Utah overview. $245 holds if the divisor is full alfalfa consumptive use (about 3 ft). The model applies it to 'forced' water, which is depletion delivered to the lake. Per AF of depletion removed, the state's 2026 study implies only 1.5 AF/ac is saved, so gross receipts lost per AF are about $500. I suggest raising high to about $500 and recording the denominator choice. I found no Hill et al. (2011) ET value in an opened source, so 3.05 ft is back-solved, not quoted.

quote: agricultural activity employed over 16,000 people and used nearly one-fifth of Utah's land
locator: article body (reporting Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute 'Portrait of Agriculture', 2022 Census basis)
publisher: Deseret News (reporting Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute)
arithmetic: 16,000 / 853,471 irrigated acres x 1000 = 18.7 jobs per 1,000 ac (model 19.2, within 3%). Using 2017 acres (1,097,219) gives 14.6.
notes: This is confirmed at about 18.7. The cited DWS page covers nonfarm jobs only. Caveats: the Gardner figure ('over 16,000') is a headcount that includes part-time labour, and nearly half worked under 150 days a year. Counting all 33,270 producers would give a far higher ratio. The numerator includes range livestock, so applying it to hay overstates losses, as the model's note says.

quote: Total Employment (Full and Part-time Jobs) Recreation Sector 1,217 236 310 1,764 / Industrial Sector 1,967 1,288 2,112 5,368 / Aquaculture (brine shrimp eggs) 373 63 138 574 / TOTAL ALL SECTORS 7,706
locator: Slide 'Estimated Total Economic Impact' (columns Direct/Indirect/Induced/Total), PDF p.24; figures from Bioeconomics Inc. 2012 (2010 data)
source_title: Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Environment Interim Committee materials (DNR Great Salt Lake presentation)

extra_sources.title: Industry and Recreation
extra_sources.quote: The Great Salt Lake contributes over $2 billion annually to Utah's economy and provides over 7,700 direct jobs.

arithmetic: Direct jobs = 1,217 + 1,967 + 373 = 3,557. Total including indirect and induced = 7,706.
notes: The only traceable figure is 7,706 total jobs (direct + indirect + induced) from the 2012 Bioeconomics study using 2010 data. The state website calls this '7,700 direct jobs', which is wrong: direct jobs are 3,557. The model's 8,650 is not in any opened source. If it comes from scaling 7,700 by a recovery share, it double-counts, because the 2010 lake was near healthy levels. US Magnesium has since closed and its rights were bought by the state, which pushes industrial jobs lower. I did not find a Gardner ~9,000-job study. I suggest 7,706 for total jobs, or 3,557 if the model wants direct jobs only.

locator: BLS QCEW 2024 annual averages, private ownership, NAICS 1121 (cattle ranching and farming) and 112 (animal production)
source_title: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, Utah 2024 annual

extra_sources.title: QCEW 2024 annual, basin counties (Box Elder 49003, Cache 49005, Salt Lake 49035, Utah 49049, Weber 49057, Davis, Morgan, Rich, Summit, Tooele, Wasatch)
extra_sources.quote: NAICS 1121 employment: Box Elder 142, Cache 173, Salt Lake 165, Utah 330 (others suppressed)

arithmetic: Utah statewide 2024 QCEW: NAICS 1121 = 1,670 jobs (beef 11211 = 594, dairy 11212 = 1,076). NAICS 112 = 2,581. Basin counties with disclosed 1121: 142 + 173 + 165 + 330 = 810, about 850–1,000 with suppressed cells. Disclosed NAICS 112 in basin counties = 1,283.
notes: The cited DWS and NASS pages hold no dairy or beef employment figure. QCEW wage-and-salary cattle employment in the basin is about 1,000 (1,670 statewide), below the model's 1,900 'at risk' value, which is itself only a share of basin employment. 1,900 is defensible only if self-employed ranch and dairy proprietors (not in QCEW) are counted, and I found no published basin count of those. The range 800–3,500 brackets the QCEW-only and with-proprietors cases. I could not trace the hard-coded 213.1 $M livestock receipts in model.ts.

quote: Those who were moderately sure their financial contributions would make a difference were willing to pay between $113 and $144 per household each year.
locator: article body; survey fielded August 2025, 1,050 respondents, manuscript under peer review
source_title: Most Utahns are willing to open their wallets to save the Great Salt Lake
publisher: Salt Lake Tribune (Weber State University study)
arithmetic: (113 + 144)/2 = 128.5, rounded to 128. Cross-check: article says 'up to $162 million per year across the state's 1.1 million households', and $162M / 1.1M = $147 per household.
notes: The value is the midpoint of the 'moderately sure' range and is confirmed. The full range runs from $36.56 (low certainty, water bill) to $485.10 (high certainty, taxes), so $113–144 is the moderate-certainty band only. The manuscript is not public yet (under peer review), so this rests on press coverage.

quote: pay an administrative fine not to exceed: (A) $5,000 for each knowing violation; or (B) $1,000 for each violation that is not knowing; (ii) replace up to 200% of water taken

extra_sources.title: Lower Colorado Basin States' Compromise on Water Conservation
extra_sources.quote: federal compensation ... for three quarters of the water savings, or 2.3 million acre-feet, which could amount to as much as $1 to $1.2 billion

arithmetic: The 200% replacement rule in $/AF is 2 AF per AF taken. At $250–380/AF lease value that is about $500–760/AF. Lower Basin compensation = $1.0–1.2B / 2.3 MAF = $435–522/AF.
notes: This is a policy choice (default 0, sweep up to 2,440 = lake value). Existing Utah enforcement is a flat per-violation fine ($1k/$5k) plus up to 200% water replacement, which works out to about $500–760/AF at current lease prices. That is a published anchor for a non-zero penalty well below the $2,440 upper sweep. Utah forfeiture law (7-year nonuse; see utah_water_right_title source) carries no $/AF penalty.
